1a.html:
A strict economic definition equates development with sustained growth of GNI and income per capita faster than population, plus structural change from agriculture to industry and services.

Why it is inadequate

  1. Averages hide distribution: GNI per capita can rise while most people stay poor, unemployed or more unequal.
  2. Income is a means, not an end: Sen shows that people convert income into well-being differently (illness, disability, climate, social norms, unequal sharing in the household).
  3. Non-income dimensions are left out: health, education, security, self-esteem, freedom of choice and the environment; poverty is multidimensional.
  4. Utility is no better: the deprived may adapt and report contentment, which hides real deprivation.

Economic development, properly understood, is growth in output together with lower poverty, unemployment and inequality (Seers) and expanded capabilities to function: being able to live long, be healthy, literate, mobile and take part in community life. Its objectives are more life-sustaining goods, higher levels of living and wider choices; in the course deck's words, economic progress with social well-being and environmental protection.

Developing economically but underdeveloped

  • Equatorial Guinea: oil gives a GNI per capita of about USD 19,500 (PPP), yet HDI is 0.591 and life expectancy 57.9 years, below Bangladesh (USD 3,677, HDI 0.608).
  • Pakistan: higher income per capita than Bangladesh (USD 5,311) but lower HDI (0.562), female literacy and child survival.
  • Hypothetical: 7% GDP growth captured by a small elite while unemployment rises, or growth that depletes forests and rivers.

So growth is necessary but not sufficient for development.
pts: States the strict economic definition: growth of GNI and income per capita with structural change
Inadequate because averages hide distribution: poverty, unemployment and inequality can worsen with growth
Inadequate because income is only a means; conversion into well-being differs (Sen)
Inadequate because it ignores health, education, freedom, self-esteem and the environment, or because utility hides deprivation
Meaning: growth with falling poverty, unemployment and inequality (Seers)
Meaning: expanding capabilities to function, or the three objectives of development
A first example (real or hypothetical) of high income with poor social outcomes, for example Equatorial Guinea (about USD 19,500, HDI 0.591), Gabon or Gulf oil states
A second example, for example Pakistan's higher income but lower HDI than Bangladesh
An example of another kind: unequal, jobless or environmentally destructive growth (real or hypothetical)
Concludes that growth is necessary but not sufficient

1a.watch:
• Three questions are printed; give each its own heading so the examiner finds them.
  • The printed "a counter may be development economically" is a misprint for "a country may be developing economically".
  • Do not stop at criticising income: the middle question asks for your own meaning of economic development.

1b.html:
In Sen's approach, a functioning is what a person achieves with the commodities they command, a "being or doing" (being nourished, literate, mobile); capabilities are the freedom to choose among functionings, given personal features and command over commodities.

Insights it gives

  1. The goal is people, not goods. Development is judged by the lives people can lead; income and growth are means.
  2. Same income, different achievement. Personal heterogeneities, environmental diversities, social climate, intra-household distribution and relational perspectives change the conversion: a person with parasites gains less from the same food.
  3. Utility is not enough. A deprived person may adapt and feel content; valuing a life is not the same as pleasure.
  4. Freedom matters. Choosing to fast differs from starving; a bike is not cycling, and cycling is not the happiness it brings.
  5. Measuring achievement. Progress is read from functionings (longevity, health, literacy), the basis of the HDI and MPI.
pts: Defines functionings (beings and doings) and capabilities (freedom to choose among functionings), with an example
Insight: development goals are expanded capabilities; income and growth are means, not ends
Insight: conversion factors (names at least three of the five) make equal incomes give unequal achievements
Insight: utility or happiness is an insufficient measure because of adaptation and valuation
Insight: freedom of choice matters (fasting against starving, or the bicycle distinction)
Achievements are measured by functionings (longevity, health, literacy), as in the HDI or MPI
1b.src: Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 16-21, 35; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 11-13
1b.watch:
• Keep the three ideas apart: having a bike (commodity), cycling (functioning) and being able to choose to cycle (capability).
  • Happiness can itself be a valued functioning (slide 21), but it is not the measure of development.

2a.fix:
• hum-ch2 slides 14 and 20 say the education index is built with a geometric mean and the maxima are the observed maxima. That was the 2010 to 2013 method. Since the 2014 Report the goalposts are fixed (85 yr, 18 yr, 15 yr, USD 75,000) and the education index is the arithmetic mean of the two schooling indices (hum-hdr p 2).
  • hum-ch2 slide 15 places "a low achievement in one dimension is not anymore linearly compensated" under the old arithmetic-mean HDI. That sentence describes the new geometric mean; the arithmetic mean assumes perfect substitutability, so a low score is fully compensated. The old HDI's 2/3 and 1/3 education weights applied to adult literacy and gross enrolment (1995 to 2009), not to mean and expected years of schooling.
2a.html:
The New Human Development Index (NHDI), introduced by UNDP in 2010, is a composite 0 to 1 index of a country's average achievement in a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living.

Step 1: dimension indices. Goalposts are the fixed minimum ("natural zero") and maximum ("aspirational target"). Each indicator is scaled to 0 to 1:

I = \frac{\text{actual value} - \text{minimum}}{\text{maximum} - \text{minimum}}
DimensionIndicatorMinimumMaximum
HealthLife expectancy at birth20 yr85 yr
KnowledgeExpected years of schooling018 yr
KnowledgeMean years of schooling015 yr
Living standardGNI per capita (2011 PPP USD)10075,000
  • The education index I_E is the arithmetic mean of the two schooling indices.
  • Income is GNI per capita at purchasing power parity (PPP: rates that equalise the cost of a common basket), in natural logs because each extra dollar adds less to capabilities:
I_I = \frac{\ln \mathrm{GNI} - \ln 100}{\ln 75{,}000 - \ln 100}

Step 2: aggregation by the geometric mean.

\mathrm{HDI} = \left(I_H \times I_E \times I_I\right)^{1/3}

This allows only imperfect substitutability: a low score in one dimension is not compensated one for one by a high score in another. Profiles (0.5, 0.6, 0.7) and (0.4, 0.6, 0.8) both average 0.6, but their geometric means are 0.594 and 0.577.

Example (Bangladesh, HDR 2019): life expectancy 72.3 yr, expected schooling 11.2 yr, mean schooling 6.1 yr, GNI per capita USD 4,057 (PPP).

\begin{aligned} I_H &= \frac{72.3-20}{85-20} = 0.805, \qquad I_E = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{11.2}{18} + \frac{6.1}{15}\right) = \frac{0.622 + 0.407}{2} = 0.514 \\ I_I &= \frac{\ln 4057 - \ln 100}{\ln 75000 - \ln 100} = 0.559, \qquad \mathrm{HDI} = (0.805 \times 0.514 \times 0.559)^{1/3} = 0.614 \end{aligned}

Classes: very high 0.800 and above, high 0.700 to 0.799, medium 0.550 to 0.699, low below 0.550; Bangladesh is medium.

New against traditional HDI: GNI replaces GDP, mean and expected schooling replace literacy and enrolment, and the geometric mean replaces the arithmetic mean.
pts: Defines the NHDI: a UNDP (2010) composite index, 0 to 1, of health, knowledge and living standard
Names the four indicators: life expectancy at birth, expected years of schooling, mean years of schooling, GNI per capita at PPP
Step 1: dimension index = (actual - minimum)/(maximum - minimum), with goalposts 20 to 85 yr, 0 to 18, 0 to 15 and USD 100 to 75,000 (the slides' observed maxima also accepted)
Education index as the mean of the two schooling indices (arithmetic mean; the slides' geometric-mean version also accepted)
Income index in natural logs because of the diminishing marginal utility of income
Step 2: \mathrm{HDI} = (I_H I_E I_I)^{1/3}, the geometric mean (cube root of the product)
Why the geometric mean: imperfect substitutability, so uneven achievement lowers the HDI (for example 0.594 and 0.577 against 0.6)
Works an example through to the HDI, for example Bangladesh 0.614 or the slides' Ghana 0.558
States the four categories with cut-offs 0.800, 0.700 and 0.550
Lists the changes from the traditional HDI: GNI for GDP, schooling years for literacy and enrolment, geometric for arithmetic mean
2a.src: Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 13-20; HDR 2019 technical notes, pp 2-3; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 14-19; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 89-90, 94
2a.watch:
• The Ghana example (hum-ch2 slide 19) uses the 2010 to 2013 version: observed maxima of 83.6 yr, 13.3 yr and USD 87,478, and an education index equal to the geometric mean of the sub-indices divided by 0.971. It also gives 0.558 when recomputed. Either version earns credit if the goalposts are stated; do not mix them.
  • Life expectancy and schooling are linear; only income is logged. An index cannot exceed 1: income above USD 75,000 is capped.
  • The arithmetic mean of the same Bangladesh indices would be 0.626, higher than 0.614: the geometric mean penalises the weak education score. The technical note, using unrounded data, gives I_E = 0.513; the HDI is 0.614 either way.
  • 0.614 is the 2018 value in the 2019 note. The latest value on hum-dim slide 20 is 0.670 (rank 129 of 193), still medium.

2b.html:
Yes: the relationship is strong and runs both ways, but it is strongest among the poor and is not automatic.

Health raises productivity and income. Healthy, well-fed workers have more energy, lose fewer sick days and learn better.

  • In Côte d'Ivoire men likely to lose a day of work a month to illness earn about 19% less.
  • In Brazil a 1% increase in height (a marker of childhood health) goes with about 7% higher wages (about 1% in the United States).
  • In Bangladesh healthier workers get better-paid jobs.
  • The effect is largest among the poorest and malnourished.

Income raises health, but weakly. The calorie income elasticity of the poor is only 0 to 0.5, and health systems matter: Sri Lanka and Kerala reached life expectancy above 70 at low incomes, richer South Africa did not.

Conclusion: the three reinforce each other, so health spending is an investment in growth, but income alone will not deliver good health.
pts: Clear answer: yes, a strong two-way relationship (health to productivity to income, and income to health)
Mechanism: energy, fewer sick days, better learning raise output per worker
Evidence: for example Côte d'Ivoire (19% lower wages), Brazil height (1% to 7%) or Bangladesh
The effect is strongest among the poorest and malnourished
Income to health is weaker: low calorie income elasticity, or health systems matter (Sri Lanka, Kerala against South Africa)
Concludes that health is an investment and income alone is not sufficient
2b.src: Ch 8 Education and health, slides 4, 25, 28; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 434-435, 470-474
2b.watch:
• Correlation is not causation: careful studies show much of the link runs from health to productivity, not only from income to health; saying so earns credit.
  • "Do you think" invites a view; a reasoned "strong but conditional" answer is ideal.

3a.html:
Project evaluation is the systematic assessment of a project's worth to its owner and to society. It is done before the project (ex-ante appraisal), during it (monitoring and mid-term evaluation) and after it (ex-post evaluation), following the stages of the project cycle.

  1. Identification. Project ideas come from plan targets, sector studies and felt needs (a flood embankment, a rural road). They are screened in a pre-feasibility study, and weak ideas are dropped early, at low cost.
  2. Preparation (feasibility study). Technical design, market or demand study, cost estimates, environmental and social impact, and the institutional set-up are worked out for alternative sites, scales and technologies. Costs and benefits are projected year by year.
  3. Appraisal (ex-ante evaluation). An independent review of the feasibility study, in steps:
    • financial analysis at market prices: is the project profitable to its owner?
    • economic analysis at shadow prices: taxes and subsidies are removed as transfers, labour and foreign exchange are valued at their opportunity cost, and externalities are added;
    • social analysis: benefits to poor groups and lagging regions get extra weight, and environmental effects are checked.

The flows are discounted and judged by NPV > 0, BCR > 1 and IRR above the social discount rate, with sensitivity tests.

  1. Approval and financing. The decision makers accept, reject or rank the project. In Bangladesh the Planning Commission appraises the proposal (DPP) and ECNEC approves the larger ones (smaller ones are approved within the Planning Ministry).
  2. Implementation and monitoring. Progress in cost, time and physical targets is tracked, and a mid-term evaluation allows correction (in Bangladesh, by IMED).
  3. Ex-post evaluation. After completion, actual costs, benefits and impacts are compared with the appraisal forecasts. The lessons feed back into the identification of new projects, closing the cycle.
pts: Defines project evaluation and its timing: ex-ante, ongoing (mid-term) and ex-post
Identification: ideas from plan priorities and needs, screened by pre-feasibility study
Preparation or feasibility study: technical, market, financial, environmental aspects of alternatives; yearly costs and benefits
Appraisal: financial analysis at market prices, economic analysis at shadow prices (transfers out, externalities in), social or distributional analysis, judged by NPV, BCR, IRR
Approval: accept, reject or rank, with the Bangladesh route (Planning Commission, ECNEC) or a general equivalent
Implementation with monitoring and mid-term evaluation for correction
Ex-post evaluation: actual results against forecasts, impact, lessons for new projects
Presents the stages as a cycle with feedback
3a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 607-610; CBA exam note, pp 2, 10-12; Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts I, IX and XII; Standard textbook treatment
3a.watch:
• The slides do not list these stages; the project cycle is the usual reading. A student who instead explains the appraisal stages (Todaro's three steps: objectives, shadow prices with a social discount rate, decision criterion; or the UNIDO financial, economic, savings, distribution and merit-good stages) should earn the stage marks.
  • Keep financial and economic analysis apart: transfers (taxes, subsidies) count in the first, not in the second.
  • The Bangladesh names (DPP, ECNEC, IMED) are the usual route for public projects; any correct general description of approval earns the mark.

3b.html:
Definitions (r = discount rate, year 0 = now):

  • NPV = \sum (B_t - C_t)/(1+r)^t = PV(B) - PV(C); accept if positive.
  • BCR = PV(B)/PV(C); accept if above 1.
  • IRR is the discount rate at which NPV = 0; accept if above the social discount rate.

Interpretation. Given: NPV = Tk 975,881.20 lakh, BCR = 1.647, IRR = 36.67%.

  • NPV: discounted benefits exceed discounted costs by Tk 975,881.20 lakh (about Tk 9,759 crore), net value added to society: accept.
  • BCR: each Tk 1 of present-value cost brings Tk 1.65 of benefit. Benefits could fall 39% (1 - 1/1.647) before BCR reaches 1.
  • IRR: the project earns 36.67% a year, far above the social discount rates commonly used (roughly 8 to 12%), so NPV stays positive for any rate below 36.67%.
  • Implied size: PV(C) = \mathrm{NPV}/(\mathrm{BCR} - 1) = 975{,}881.20/0.647 = 1{,}508{,}317 lakh Tk.

Answer: all three criteria agree: the project is viable and should be approved.
pts: NPV defined as PV(B) - PV(C) with the formula; accept if positive
BCR defined as PV(B)/PV(C); accept if above 1
IRR defined as the rate giving NPV = 0; accept if above the discount rate
NPV: PV of benefits exceeds PV of costs by Tk 975,881.20 lakh, net value added, accept
BCR 1.647: Tk 1.65 of benefit per Tk 1 of cost; a margin of about 39% on benefits (or the implied PV of costs, about Tk 1,508,317 lakh)
IRR 36.67% far above the social discount rate; robust to the choice of rate
Concludes that all three agree and the project should be approved
3b.src: CBA exam note, pp 5-9; Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts IV, V, VII and X; Standard textbook treatment
3b.watch:
• Tk 975,881.20 lakh is Tk 9,759 crore: one lakh is 100,000 and one crore is 100 lakh.
  • The implied PV of costs assumes the gross BCR PV(B)/PV(C) at the same discount rate as the NPV.
  • With 8.33 marks, keep the definitions to one line each and spend the time on the interpretation.

4a.html:
A single theory that fits every developing country is unlikely; a shared framework, applied country by country, is realistic.

Why diversity defeats one theory. Developing countries differ in size (China against Bhutan), resources (Gulf oil against resource-poor Bangladesh), colonial history and institutions, ethnic and religious make-up, the weight of agriculture and the informal sector, the roles of state and market, political systems, and dependence on foreign trade and capital. So the factor that most limits growth differs: saving in one country, skills or infrastructure in another, governance or conflict in a third.

Each classic theory explains part of the story

  • Linear stages (Rostow, Harrod-Domar): investment matters, but it is necessary, not sufficient; the Marshall Plan worked only where institutions existed.
  • Structural change (Lewis, Chenery): fits labour-surplus economies such as China, but many countries have little rural surplus labour and much urban unemployment.
  • Dependence: international power can constrain development, but globally integrated countries (South Korea, Taiwan) grew fast.
  • Neoclassical (market fundamentalism): governments fail, but markets fail too; East Asia shows a constructive role for the state.

The slides conclude that development economics has no universally accepted paradigm: each theory has strengths and weaknesses, and insights keep evolving.

The case for some unity. Common elements recur: capital accumulation, human capital, technology, sound institutions, macroeconomic stability and a balance of market and state. Newer approaches (endogenous growth, coordination failure, and growth diagnostics that find each country's binding constraint) combine them into one method, not one recipe.

Conclusion: a unified set of questions is possible, but not a single theory prescribing one path; policy must fit each country's institutions and politics.
pts: Clear position (no single theory, or a qualified yes), argued from the diversity of countries
Names at least four dimensions of diversity (size, resources, history and institutions, ethnic or social structure, sector structure, politics, external dependence)
Explains that the binding constraint differs between countries, so prescriptions differ
Stages theory: what it explains (investment) and its limit (not sufficient)
Structural change: what it explains (labour transfer) and its limit (no rural surplus, urban unemployment)
Dependence: what it explains (international power) and its limit (successful integrated economies)
Neoclassical: what it explains (government failure, prices) and its limit (market failure, East Asia)
States that there is no universally accepted paradigm; each theory has strengths and weaknesses
Counterpoint: common principles or a shared method (growth diagnostics, endogenous growth) give some unity
Conclusion consistent with the position
4a.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 2, 20-21, 27, 30-35; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 168-170, 174-176, 181-182
4a.watch:
• A reasoned "yes, at a high level of generality" also earns full marks if it admits that country-specific policy is still needed.
  • Do not just describe the four theories; tie each to why it cannot cover all countries.
  • Growth diagnostics and coordination failure come from Todaro chapter 4, beyond the chapter 3 slides; they are an addition, not a requirement.

4b.html:
Dependence is the reliance of developing countries on rich countries' markets, capital and policies for their own growth; the rich countries' greater power over trade, prices and finance is dominance.

Developing countries depend on rich ones for:

  • Export markets and foreign exchange: Bangladesh's garments, 84% of its exports, sell mainly to the EU and USA.
  • Finance: aid, loans and foreign direct investment, which leave external debt.
  • Technology, skills and policy: machinery and training, and IMF or World Bank conditions and advice.

Rich countries depend on developing ones for:

  • Raw materials and energy: oil, gas, cobalt, rare earths.
  • Cheap manufactures within global supply chains (garments, electronics, parts).
  • Markets and profits: growing middle classes buy rich-country goods; multinationals repatriate profits.
  • Labour and global public goods: migrant workers, and cooperation on climate and disease control.

So the relationship is interdependence, but unequal: developing countries depend more and have less bargaining power.
pts: Defines dependence (reliance on rich-country markets, capital and policies), with dominance
Developing countries depend on rich export markets, with an example (garments to the EU and USA)
Developing countries depend on aid, loans or foreign investment
Developing countries depend on rich-country technology, skills or policy advice and conditions
Opposite: rich countries need raw materials and energy
Opposite: rich countries rely on cheap manufactures and supply chains
Opposite: developing countries are markets and a source of profits
Opposite: migrant labour or global public goods such as climate and health
Concludes that the relationship is interdependence, but unequal
4b.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slide 30; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 170-171, 174, 185; Bangladesh and the SDGs (2026), slide 6
4b.watch:
• The same question was set in 2020-21 (Q4b); the marks are printed as 8.33 and the points total 8.5.
  • Half the marks are for "the opposite": give at least three ways rich countries depend on developing ones.

5a.html:
The Gini coefficient is a one-number summary of the Lorenz curve: it measures how far the curve lies from the line of equality.

Lorenz curve. People ranked from poorest to richest; cumulative % of population on the horizontal axis, cumulative % of income on the vertical. The diagonal is perfect equality.

Gini from the Lorenz curve. With A the area between the diagonal and the curve and B the area under the curve:

G = \frac{A}{A + B}, \qquad A + B = \tfrac{1}{2} \;\Rightarrow\; G = 1 - 2B

(axes as fractions from 0 to 1).

The relationship

  • Curve on the diagonal: A = 0, so G = 0 (perfect equality).
  • Curve along the bottom and right-hand axes: B = 0, so G = 1 (perfect inequality).
  • The more the curve bows, the larger A and the higher G. In Table 5.1 the bottom 50% gets 19.8% of income and G \approx 0.44.
  • From grouped data B is a sum of trapezoids: G = 1 - \sum (X_k - X_{k-1})(Y_k + Y_{k-1}).

Not one-to-one. Each Lorenz curve gives one Gini, but one Gini fits many curves: two crossing curves can have the same Gini. The Lorenz criterion ranks distributions only when curves do not cross; the Gini always gives a ranking, at the cost of a value judgement about where inequality matters.
pts: Describes the Lorenz curve: cumulative population against cumulative income, diagonal = equality
Gini = area between the diagonal and the Lorenz curve over the total area under the diagonal, A/(A+B)
Since A + B = 1/2, G = 1 - 2B (or twice the area A)
Limits: curve on the diagonal gives 0; curve along the axes gives 1
The more bowed the curve, the larger A and the higher the Gini (Table 5.1, about 0.44, as an illustration only)
Computing B from grouped data by trapezoids, or by reading areas off the diagram
Not one-to-one: crossing Lorenz curves can share a Gini; Lorenz ranking is partial, Gini ranking complete
5a.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 9-15; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 265-269
5a.watch:
• "Relationship" asks how one is obtained from the other; defining the two separately without linking them through the areas earns little.
  • The Gini is a ratio of areas, not the maximum gap between the curve and the diagonal.

5b.html:
The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of population, ranked from the poorest; the Gini coefficient is the area between the curve and the diagonal over the whole triangle, G = A/(A+B), from 0 (equality) to 1. Together they summarise a whole distribution.

Example 1: comparing nations at one time. Quintile shares (Table 5.2) give cumulative income at 20, 40, 60, 80% of population of 9.4, 22.0, 38.1, 59.2% for Bangladesh (2005) and 5.4, 16.1, 31.8, 54.2% for the United States (2000).

  • Bangladesh's curve lies above the US curve everywhere, so by the Lorenz criterion it is unambiguously more equal.
  • The Gini puts a number on it: 0.29 against 0.37 from these quintiles (survey values 0.32 and 0.415). Japan, whose richest 20% get 35.7%, is more equal still; Brazil, at 58.7%, much less.

Example 2: judging the distribution as a nation grows. Fields' growth typologies shift the Lorenz curve:

  • Traditional-sector enrichment: the curve moves up toward the diagonal, so inequality falls.
  • Modern-sector enrichment: the curve moves down, so inequality rises.
  • Modern-sector enlargement (Lewis): the new and old curves cross, so the Lorenz criterion cannot rank them. A summary measure such as the Gini decides, and plotting the Gini against GNI per capita gives the Kuznets inverted U.

Limit. Both measure relative inequality only: Brazil and Mexico had the same income per head (USD 8,610) but Gini values of 53.7 and 43.4.
pts: Defines the Lorenz curve (cumulative population against cumulative income, diagonal = equality)
Defines the Gini, A/(A+B), 0 to 1
Example 1 set out: a comparison of two countries with data or a sketch (for example Bangladesh and the US, or Japan and Brazil)
Uses Lorenz dominance: the higher curve is unambiguously more equal
Uses the Gini values to rank them (for example 0.29 against 0.37)
Example 2 set out: a second sound use, for example one country's distribution over time or with growth (Fields' typologies), the Kuznets plot, or land or education distribution
Explains crossing Lorenz curves and the need for the Gini (or another measure) to rank them
Links the Gini to income level (Kuznets curve) or notes that it ignores the income level
5b.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 9-15, 31, 34-42; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 265-268, 276-284
5b.watch:
• Any two sound examples earn the credit: two countries compared, one country over time, the Kuznets plot of Gini against income, or Lorenz curves for land or education.
  • The quintile Ginis (0.29, 0.37) sit below the survey values (0.32, 0.415) partly because five points ignore inequality within each fifth, and partly because the survey values are for later years.

6a.html:
Tied aid is foreign aid, in the form of bilateral grants or loans, that the recipient must use to buy goods and services from the donor country, or only for a project the donor specifies.

  • Tied by source: the money must be spent on the donor's goods, contractors or consultants, for example an Indian line of credit that requires most procurement from India.
  • Tied by project: the money can only finance a named project, such as a road or power plant.

Untied aid may be spent with the cheapest supplier anywhere. Donors tie aid to help their exporters; it lowers the aid's real value, as the donor's source is usually dearer.
pts: Defines tied aid: aid that must be spent on donor-country goods and services or on donor-specified projects
Distinguishes tying by source and by project
Contrasts with untied aid, spendable anywhere
Notes why it matters: higher cost and lower real value, and the donor's export motive
6a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 807, 813
6a.watch:
• Do not confuse tying with conditionality: conditions attach policies to aid, tying restricts where it is spent.
  • A one-line definition earns most of the marks; the example and the contrast with untied aid secure the rest.

6b.html:
Tied aid must be spent on goods and services from the donor country or on donor-specified projects. The shift from grants to loans and from untied to tied aid makes aid serve the donor more and the recipient less.

Disadvantages of tied aid

  1. Higher prices. The recipient cannot buy from the cheapest supplier; donor firms are often costly or monopolistic. Studies put the extra cost at roughly 15 to 30%, so the real value of aid falls below its face value.
  2. Inappropriate technology. Capital-intensive equipment suited to the donor creates few jobs in a labour-abundant country and ties the recipient to the donor's spare parts and experts.
  3. Distorted priorities. Donors pick showcase projects that suit their firms; machinery may be bought while existing plants run below capacity, and maintenance is neglected.
  4. Aid flows back to the donor through its consultants, contractors and shipping: an export subsidy for the donor.
  5. Delays and leverage. Donor procurement rules slow projects, and conditions reduce policy freedom.

Extra burden when the aid is an interest-bearing loan

  1. The overpricing is borrowed: the recipient repays the inflated cost with interest, so the grant element shrinks further.
  2. Foreign-exchange drain: repayment in dollars uses export earnings, often for projects that earn only local currency, so the foreign-exchange gap widens later.
  3. Exchange-rate risk: as the taka fell from about Tk 86 to about Tk 120 per US dollar (2022 to 2024), the taka cost of repayment rose by about 40%.
  4. Debt accumulation: Bangladesh's external debt service rose to about USD 3.36 billion in FY2023-24 as grace periods ended; Sri Lanka's 2022 default shows the extreme case of debt service outrunning foreign-exchange earnings.

Conclusion: tied loans give less development per dollar and leave debt; recipients should seek untied, highly concessional finance and borrow only where returns cover the full cost.
pts: Defines tied aid (donor-country procurement or donor-specified projects) and notes the shift to tied loans
Higher prices from no competitive procurement, lowering real value (the 15 to 30% estimate is optional)
Inappropriate capital-intensive technology, few jobs, dependence on donor parts and experts
Distorted priorities: donor-chosen projects, idle capacity or neglected maintenance
Aid returns to donor firms and consultants, or delays and political leverage
Loans: the inflated cost is repaid with interest, so the grant element shrinks
Loans: debt service in foreign exchange drains export earnings and widens the foreign-exchange gap
Loans: exchange-rate risk raises the local-currency cost of repayment
Loans: debt accumulation (an example is optional) and a conclusion on better terms

7a.html:
Industrialisation is the structural shift of output, exports and jobs towards manufacturing. Bangladesh's industry is over a third of GDP, led by ready-made garments (RMG, about 84% of exports). Its prospects are good:

  1. Demographic dividend. A young labour force of 7.35 crore (2023), rising each year, with low wages: an advantage in labour-intensive manufacturing as China's wages rise.
  2. A proven export industry. Bangladesh is one of the two largest garment exporters and has many certified green factories; it can move up to man-made-fibre and higher-value clothing, and RMG's backward linkages (spinning, dyeing, accessories, packaging) widen the base.
  3. Emerging sectors: pharmaceuticals (most domestic demand met, growing exports), leather and footwear, light engineering, shipbuilding, electronics and ICT services.
  4. Infrastructure and zones: the Padma Bridge, Karnaphuli tunnel, Matarbari deep-sea port and new power plants cut costs; the planned 100 economic zones and hi-tech parks offer serviced land.
  5. Markets: over 170 million consumers with rising, remittance-fed incomes; nearness to India, China and ASEAN; duty-free access to the EU during the transition after LDC graduation.
  6. Agro-processing: surpluses of rice, fish, vegetables and fruit can feed food-processing industries.
  7. Policy support: bonded warehouses, back-to-back letters of credit, export incentives and the digital and 4IR agenda.

Conclusion: Bangladesh has the labour, the export experience and the new infrastructure to industrialise further, provided it diversifies beyond garments.
pts: Defines industrialisation and states the current base (industry over a third of GDP, RMG dominant)
Demographic dividend: large, young, low-wage labour force
Established RMG industry with room to upgrade, green factories or backward linkages
Emerging sectors such as pharmaceuticals, leather, light engineering, shipbuilding or ICT
New infrastructure and economic zones lowering costs
Large domestic market or regional and preferential export markets
Agro-processing from farm surpluses
Policy support (bonded warehouses, back-to-back LCs, incentives) and a conclusion on diversification

  • The challenges are part (b) of the same question; do not spend this part on them.

7b.html:
The main challenges of industrialisation in Bangladesh are:

  1. Narrow base: RMG earns about 84% of exports, mostly from the EU and USA, so a shock to one product or market hits the whole economy.
  2. Energy and land: gas shortages, load-shedding, costly imported fuel and scarce industrial land raise costs and deter investment.
  3. Investment climate: red tape, corruption, slow contract enforcement and policy uncertainty; private investment is stuck near 23% of GDP and FDI below 1% of GDP.
  4. Finance: high non-performing loans weaken banks, credit goes to a few large borrowers, and the dollar shortage since 2022 hampers imports of machinery and raw materials.
  5. Skills and technology: low labour productivity, weak technical education, few engineers and managers, and the threat of automation to low-skill jobs.
  6. LDC graduation (scheduled for 2026): loss of duty-free access in some markets and of policy space, such as the patent waiver for pharmaceuticals and export subsidies.
  7. Safety and environment: the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse (over 1,100 deaths) and river pollution from dyeing and tanneries threaten buyers' confidence.

Conclusion: these constraints, not the lack of potential, limit Bangladesh's industrial growth.
pts: Narrow, RMG-dependent export base and market concentration
Energy, gas, power or land shortages
Poor investment climate: bureaucracy, corruption, low private investment or FDI
Financial-sector weakness or foreign-exchange shortage
Low skills, productivity or technology, or automation risk
LDC graduation: loss of preferences and policy space
Workplace safety or environmental pollution
Concludes that constraints, not potential, limit industrialisation

8a.fix: • Slide 5 of the SDG deck lists SDG 13 both as the one achieved goal and among nine "stagnating" goals (5, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17), so its four groups add to 18 goals. With SDG 13 counted once as achieved, eight goals are stagnating (47%), not nine (52.9%).
8a.html:
Not all of them. Bangladesh can meet several SDG targets by 2030, but on present trends not the full agenda.

Evidence of progress

  • SDG 13 is rated achieved; SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 are moderately improving.
  • Poverty fell to 18.7% (2022), electricity access is 96%, primary enrolment above 97% and under-5 mortality 29 per 1,000, close to the target of 25.

Why full achievement is unlikely

  • Pace: only 20.8% of targets are on track; the SDG Index score is 63.9 (rank 114 of 167). Eight goals are stagnating and two (11 cities, 16 institutions) are getting worse.
  • Finance: about USD 132.6 billion a year extra is needed to 2030, but tax revenue is below 8% of GDP.
  • Gaps: maternal mortality is 169 per 100,000 against a target of 70; inequality is widening; data are missing for many indicators.
  • Risks: climate shocks, LDC graduation (lost trade preferences) and weak governance.

Conclusion: some goals are within reach, but meeting all of them by 2030 needs revenue reform, better data, local delivery, climate finance and private investment.
pts: Clear judgement: some goals or targets reachable, the full agenda unlikely (a reasoned "yes, with conditions" also earns this)
Evidence of progress: improving goals and indicators (poverty, electricity, enrolment, child mortality)
Evidence of shortfall: 20.8% of targets on track, index score 63.9 or rank 114, stagnating and declining goals
Financing constraint: USD 132.6 billion a year gap, tax-to-GDP below 8%
Other constraints: governance, inequality, climate, data gaps or LDC graduation
Conclusion with the actions needed
8a.watch:
• "Explain" needs evidence both ways and a judgement; a bare "yes" or "no" earns little.
  • SDG 13 is rated achieved mainly because Bangladesh's emissions per person are low; its climate adaptation needs are still large.

8b.html:
Yes, partly. The Padma Bridge and the Metro Rail are infrastructure: they enable progress on several SDGs but cannot achieve them alone.

The Padma Multipurpose Bridge (6.15 km; road from 2022, rail from 2023) links about 21 south-western districts and Mongla and Payra ports to Dhaka. The Metro Rail (MRT Line 6, Uttara to Motijheel) is Dhaka's first electric mass transit.

Goals and how

  • SDG 9 (infrastructure, industrialisation): both are resilient core infrastructure; Padma opens the south-west to industry and port trade.
  • SDG 8 (growth, jobs): cheaper, faster transport raises trade and investment; appraisals expected Padma to add about 1.2% to GDP.
  • SDGs 1, 2 and 10: south-western farmers and fishers reach Dhaka markets quickly, earn more, and the regional gap narrows.
  • SDG 11 (cities): Metro gives safe, affordable public transport and less congestion.
  • SDGs 13 and 3: electric trains cut emissions and air pollution; both reduce accidents and speed access to hospitals.
  • SDG 5: safer travel widens women's access to jobs and study.

Limits. High cost and foreign loans (Metro), one metro line, tolls and fares the poor may not afford, and land acquisition. Benefits need economic zones, power, skills and good maintenance.

Conclusion: they directly advance SDGs 8, 9 and 11 and indirectly 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 and 13; other goals need other policies.
pts: Clear position: they help, as enablers rather than a full route to the SDGs
Describes the two projects and their reach
SDG 9: resilient infrastructure and industrialisation, explained
SDG 8: growth, trade, investment or jobs
SDGs 1, 2 and 10: market access, rural incomes, regional inequality
SDG 11: safe, affordable urban transport and less congestion
SDG 13, 3 or 5: emissions, air quality, safety or women's mobility
Limits: cost and debt, coverage, affordability, need for complementary policies
Conclusion naming the goals helped directly and those needing other measures
